questions.question: A bank's DevOps team wants Claude Code to run in CI on every pull request, triage failing tests, and pass a machine-readable result to the next pipeline step, without granting broader access than needed. Which TWO configuration choices best meet these goals? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Run Claude Code in non-interactive print mode with an explicit, minimal allowed-tools list for the triage job.
Start an interactive Claude Code session on the build agent and have the pipeline type the prompt into it.
Request JSON output so the next pipeline step can parse the result instead of scraping free-form text.
Turn on the bypass-permissions mode so the job never stalls waiting for an approval prompt in CI.
Allow every available tool for the job so that Claude never fails because a tool it wanted was missing.

questions.explanation: Print mode (-p) is built for scripted, non-interactive runs, and an explicit allowed-tools list approves only what the triage job needs. JSON output gives the next step structured data to parse. Driving an interactive session from a script is fragile. Bypassing permissions or allowing every tool grants far more access than the job requires.

questions.question: A team's CLAUDE.md says to run the code formatter after every edit, but Claude still skips it now and then, and pull requests fail the format check. The team wants the formatter to run every single time. What should they do?

options.text: Rewrite the CLAUDE.md formatting instruction in capital letters and move it to the top of the file.
Configure a PostToolUse hook on file edits and writes that runs the formatter automatically.
Ask reviewers to run the formatter by hand on each pull request before they approve it.
Create a subagent whose only job is to remind the main agent to run the formatter after it edits files.

questions.explanation: Hooks run deterministically on lifecycle events, so a PostToolUse hook on edit and write tools guarantees the formatter runs after every change. Stronger CLAUDE.md wording is still guidance the model may not follow. Manual reviewer steps move the work back to people. A reminder subagent is another probabilistic layer, with extra cost and complexity.

questions.question: A developer asks Claude Code to work out why a nightly job is slow. Investigating means reading several large log files and test outputs, and the main conversation quickly fills with output that won't be needed again. What is the best way to keep the main session focused?

options.text: Run the compact command after every log file so that the main conversation stays inside the window.
Switch the main session to a larger model so that it can absorb all of the log output without degrading.
Paste all the log files into the main conversation at once so that Claude sees everything together.
Delegate the log analysis to a subagent so that it reads the logs in its own context and returns a summary.

questions.explanation: Subagents run in their own context window, so verbose log and test output stays out of the main conversation and only a summary comes back. Compacting repeatedly loses detail and treats the symptom. A larger model doesn't stop the noise from crowding out useful context. Pasting everything at once makes the clutter worse.

questions.question: A senior engineer will use Claude Code to refactor the authentication module of a payments service, a high-risk change touching many files. Which TWO workflow practices best improve the outcome? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Use plan mode first so Claude explores the code and proposes a plan for review before it edits anything.
Paste the entire repository into the first prompt so that Claude has all of the code in context at once.
Run the session with permission checks bypassed so Claude can make all edits without stopping to ask.
Give Claude a way to verify its work, such as running the authentication test suite after each change.
Keep correcting Claude in the same long session, no matter how many failed attempts have built up.

questions.explanation: Plan mode separates exploration from editing, so the approach can be reviewed before risky changes, and a verification signal such as tests lets Claude check its own work. Pasting the whole repo floods the context instead of letting Claude read what it needs. Bypassing permissions removes oversight on a high-risk change. Long sessions full of failed attempts degrade performance, and the docs advise clearing and restarting with a better prompt.

questions.question: Engineers at a media company write release notes with the same multi-step procedure: gather merged PRs, group them by area, apply the style guide, and flag breaking changes. Each person prompts Claude Code differently and quality varies. What is the best way to standardize this?

options.text: Create a project Skill for the release-notes procedure, committed to the repository, that engineers can invoke.
Add the full procedure to the project CLAUDE.md so that it is loaded into every session in the repository.
Publish the procedure on the internal wiki and ask engineers to copy it into their prompts when needed.
Add a SessionStart hook that prints the entire procedure at the start of every Claude Code session.

questions.explanation: A project Skill packages a repeatable procedure that loads only when invoked or relevant, and committing it gives everyone the same version. Putting it in CLAUDE.md, or printing it at every session start, costs context in every session, including the many that have nothing to do with release notes. A wiki relies on manual copying, which is how the inconsistency started.

questions.question: A team added an internal MCP server to the repository's .mcp.json. Most developers see its tools, but one developer's Claude Code session shows none of them, and the server definition is identical for everyone. What is the best first diagnostic step for that developer?

options.text: Reinstall Claude Code from scratch, because missing MCP tools usually indicate a corrupted installation.
Ask the server owners to rewrite the MCP server, since it evidently fails for some clients but not others.
Run /mcp to check the server's status and approve it if its one-time project approval was dismissed.
Add the server's tool names to the developer's allowed-tools list so that Claude Code can load them.

questions.explanation: /mcp shows each server's connection and approval status, and a dismissed one-time approval for a project-scoped server is a documented reason a correctly defined server provides no tools. Reinstalling or rewriting the server skips cheap diagnosis and targets the wrong component. Allow rules control permission to call tools that are already loaded; they don't load a server that hasn't been approved.

questions.question: A developer added a PreToolUse hook meant to block edits to migration files, but edits still go through and the hook never seems to run. What is the most effective way to diagnose this?

options.text: Replace the hook with a CLAUDE.md instruction, since instructions are easier to debug than hooks are.
Run /hooks to confirm the hook is registered, then start a session with --debug to watch it being evaluated.
Increase the hook's timeout value, since hooks that never fire are usually being cut off before finishing.
Reinstall Claude Code and recreate the project settings, since hooks that don't fire mean a broken install.

questions.explanation: The documented approach is to check /hooks to see whether Claude Code loaded the hook (common causes include a matcher written as an array or hooks in a standalone file), then use --debug to watch evaluation live. A CLAUDE.md instruction swaps a deterministic control for a probabilistic one. A timeout only matters for a hook that runs. Reinstalling skips diagnosis entirely.

questions.question: A VP of engineering wants organization-wide visibility into Claude Code usage, including cost by team, sessions, and tool acceptance rates, to spot problems and plan capacity. The company already runs an OpenTelemetry-compatible observability stack. What should the platform team do?

options.text: Survey developers each month about how often they use Claude Code and how much they think it costs them.
Ask each developer to paste the output of the cost command into a shared spreadsheet at the end of every week.
Write a script that parses developers' shell histories to count how often the claude command is launched.
Enable Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export through managed settings and send it to the existing stack.

questions.explanation: Claude Code can export metrics and events through OpenTelemetry, and setting the telemetry variables in managed settings applies them consistently across the organization, feeding the existing stack. Surveys and self-reported spreadsheets are incomplete and unreliable. Parsing shell histories is invasive and doesn't capture cost or tool decisions.

questions.question: During a production incident, an on-call engineer at a payments company wants Claude Code to help find out why API errors spiked after the latest deploy. The team cannot risk Claude changing production systems during the investigation. What is the best way to use Claude Code here?

options.text: Give Claude production credentials and bypass permissions so it can find and apply a fix as fast as possible.
Give Claude the error logs and the deploy diff, keep it to read-only tools, and ask for evidence-based root causes.
Ask Claude why production is broken without sharing any logs, so its analysis is not biased by the symptoms.
Ask Claude to restart every production service first, then investigate the cause once things stabilize.

questions.explanation: Concrete evidence (errors and the recent diff) lets Claude reason about the actual root cause, and limiting it to read-only tools honors the no-changes constraint during an incident. Production credentials with bypassed permissions are exactly the risk the team ruled out. Withholding the logs leaves Claude guessing. Blind restarts are an unreviewed production change that can destroy diagnostic state.

questions.question: A bank's internal analytics assistant has 40 tools from five MCP servers. Traces show it frequently picks the wrong tool for revenue questions because three tools overlap: a generic SQL runner, a revenue-report tool, and a CSV-export tool that can all return revenue figures. What change most directly fixes the misselection?

options.text: Add a system prompt section that ranks the three overlapping tools by preference for each kind of revenue question the team receives.
Upgrade the assistant to the largest available model so it can disambiguate overlapping tools better.
Consolidate the overlapping functionality into one clearly scoped revenue tool and remove the redundant paths.
Add several few-shot examples to the prompt showing the correct tool choice for common revenue queries.

questions.explanation: Overlapping tools create ambiguous choices; if a human engineer cannot say which tool applies, the model cannot either, so the root-cause fix is to remove the overlap and leave one clearly scoped tool. Preference rankings (A) and few-shot examples (D) are probabilistic patches that leave the ambiguity in place and cost tokens on every request. A larger model (B) may guess better but still faces the same redundant options and adds cost.

questions.question: An insurer's claims orchestrator spawns a summarization subagent that only reads claim files and writes a summary back to the orchestrator. Because no tool list was set for it, the subagent inherits every tool the orchestrator has, including tools that update claim status and issue payments. What is the best configuration change?

options.text: Give the summarization subagent an explicit allowlist containing only the read tools its task requires.
Add a line to the subagent's system prompt stating that it must never call the status-update or payment tools under any circumstances.
Keep the inherited tools but log every call the subagent makes so reviewers can audit misuse later.
Run the subagent on a smaller, cheaper model so any accidental tool calls cost less to execute.

questions.explanation: Each agent in a multi-agent system should receive only the capabilities its role needs, and an explicit tool allowlist removes the write and payment capabilities from the subagent entirely. A prompt instruction (B) is a probabilistic control that a prompt injection in a claim file could override. Logging (C) is detective, not preventive, and a cheaper model (D) does nothing to narrow what the subagent is allowed to do.

questions.question: A vendor's MCP server for a scheduling system mirrors its REST API one-to-one, exposing about 60 endpoints such as list_users, list_events, get_availability, and create_event. To book a single meeting the agent makes eight or more calls and fills its context with raw intermediate results. Which redesign best addresses the problem?

options.text: Raise the agent's max_tokens limit so long chains of scheduling calls have enough room to complete.
Enable parallel tool calls so the agent can issue all eight lookups at the same time instead of waiting on each one in sequence.
Increase the MCP output token limit so complete raw responses are returned without being truncated.
Wrap the commonly chained steps in a task-level tool, such as schedule_meeting, that returns a concise result.

questions.explanation: Tools that mirror low-level API endpoints push orchestration onto the model; consolidating frequently chained steps into a single task-level tool cuts calls and keeps intermediate data out of context. Higher max_tokens (A) or a higher output limit (C) accommodates the bloat instead of removing it. Parallel calls (B) can reduce latency but still put all the raw intermediate results into context.

questions.question: A security review of a hospital's patient-services agent finds that six of its 25 tools are administrative tools no workflow has called in six months, and that its patient-lookup tool returns the full medical record when the agent only ever needs appointment status. Which TWO changes best reduce capability bloat and exposure? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Rewrite every tool description in more detail so the model is less likely to call the administrative tools by mistake.
Remove the six unused administrative tools from the agent's configuration rather than leaving them available.
Mark all 25 tools for deferred loading so their definitions are only loaded into context after a search.
Narrow the lookup tool's response to the fields the workflow needs, such as appointment status and time.
Add a dashboard that tracks how often each tool is called so the team can spot unexpected usage.

questions.explanation: Removing unused tools eliminates capability the agent does not need, and narrowing the response stops unnecessary PHI from entering the context at all. Better descriptions (A) still leave the capabilities reachable. Deferred loading (C) is a context-management technique; deferred tools can still be discovered and called, so it does not reduce what the agent is able to do. A usage dashboard (E) is monitoring, not a reduction in exposure.

questions.question: A retailer's customer-service agent uses eight narrow, typed tools for order lookups (by order ID, by email, and so on). An engineer proposes replacing them with one execute_sql tool against the production database to reduce tool count. How should the architect evaluate the proposal?

options.text: Reject it as proposed; consolidate into one typed order-lookup tool against a read-only order view instead.
Approve it, because fewer tools always improve tool selection accuracy and reduce prompt tokens.
Approve it, provided the system prompt instructs the agent to run only SELECT statements against the order-related tables.
Reject it, and keep all eight narrow tools exactly as they are, since consolidation is never appropriate.

questions.explanation: Consolidation is good when it removes overlap, but a raw SQL tool widens capability far beyond the role, exposing every table and write access to a model reading untrusted customer input. A single typed lookup tool against a read-only view gets the reduced tool count without the privilege expansion. Approving outright (B) ignores the new attack surface, and a prompt rule (C) is not an enforceable control. Refusing any consolidation (D) misses a legitimate simplification.

questions.question: An HR team built a remote MCP server in front of its payroll API. The server accepts any valid access token issued by the corporate identity provider and forwards that same token to the payroll API on each request. What is the most significant security gap?

options.text: The tokens may have lifetimes that are too long, so the identity provider should issue shorter-lived tokens.
The server does not check that tokens were issued for it, and it passes client tokens through to the payroll API.
The server should require mutual TLS between the MCP client and server in addition to bearer tokens.
The server should restrict incoming requests to IP address ranges that belong to the corporate network and approved partner VPNs.

questions.explanation: The MCP authorization spec requires servers to validate that tokens were issued specifically for them as the audience and forbids passing a client's token through to upstream APIs; the server must obtain its own token for the payroll API. Accepting any corporate token and forwarding it creates confused-deputy and token-reuse risk. Shorter lifetimes (A), mTLS (C), and IP restrictions (D) are reasonable hardening, but none fixes the audience and passthrough flaw.

questions.question: A professional services firm deploys an internal knowledge agent that searches the document store with a single service account that can read every matter. Testing shows any employee can retrieve documents from matters they are walled off from. What is the best fix?

options.text: Instruct the agent in its system prompt to decline requests for documents from restricted matters.
Pass every generated answer through a redaction classifier that strips content from any matter the requesting user is walled off from.
Deploy a separate agent per practice group, each still using the same service account for retrieval.
Carry the end user's identity into retrieval and enforce the store's access controls before results reach the model.

questions.explanation: The gap is that authorization is evaluated for the agent's service account rather than the requesting user, so the fix is to propagate user identity and filter results by that user's permissions at the retrieval layer, before content reaches the model. Prompt instructions (A) and output classifiers (B) are probabilistic and act after restricted content is already in context. Splitting agents (C) still uses an all-access identity, so the wall is still not enforced.

questions.question: A fintech agent reads inbound customer emails and has a tool that issues refunds. Red-teamers show that an email containing hidden instructions can get the agent to refund a different customer's order. Which control best closes the authorization gap?

options.text: Enforce refund authorization in application code, checking the order belongs to the authenticated sender and is within policy limits.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to ignore any instructions that appear inside email bodies.
Move the agent to a more capable model that is better at resisting prompt injection attempts.
Log every refund along with the email that triggered it, so the fraud team can identify and reverse any unauthorized refunds afterward.

questions.explanation: Untrusted content should never be able to authorize a privileged action; a deterministic check in the tool's implementation, tying the refund to the authenticated customer's own order and to policy limits, holds regardless of what the model is persuaded to do. Prompt instructions (B) and a stronger model (C) lower the odds of injection but cannot guarantee it is resisted. Logging (D) only detects the loss after the fact.

questions.question: A bank's platform team finds that developers have committed a shared .mcp.json for Claude Code that contains a production database password with write access. What is the best remediation?

options.text: Move the file into .gitignore so it is no longer tracked, and keep using the same shared password locally.
Remove the secret, rotate it, and use environment variable expansion so each developer supplies their own scoped credential.
Keep the file in the repository but encrypt it so that only developers with the decryption key can read it.
Replace the password with a long-lived API key that carries the same database permissions but is easier for the platform team to rotate.

questions.explanation: Claude Code supports environment variable expansion in .mcp.json so teams can share server configuration without committing secrets, and each developer can supply an individually scoped, ideally read-only, credential. The leaked password must also be rotated because it is already in git history. Ignoring the file (A) leaves the exposed shared secret in use. Encrypting a shared credential (C) or swapping in an equally privileged key (D) keeps the over-privileged shared identity in place.

questions.question: A logistics company exposes a remote MCP server to partners using OAuth. An audit finds that the partner desktop client sends access tokens as a URL query parameter and runs the authorization code flow without PKCE. Which TWO changes bring the integration in line with the MCP authorization specification? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Send access tokens only in the Authorization request header using the Bearer scheme.
Switch partners to the stdio transport so that no tokens ever travel over the network.
Replace OAuth with long-lived static API keys issued to each partner organization.
Have the MCP server forward each partner's token to internal APIs to preserve identity.
Implement PKCE in the client's authorization code flow to protect against code interception.

questions.explanation: The MCP authorization spec requires clients to send tokens in the Authorization Bearer header and never in the query string, and requires PKCE to prevent authorization code interception. Stdio (B) is for local processes on the same machine and does not apply to remote partners. Static long-lived keys (C) weaken security, and token passthrough (D) is explicitly forbidden by the spec.

questions.question: A telecom's voice IVR uses Claude to route each caller utterance to one of 12 intents. The current configuration, the largest model at high effort, is 97% accurate on the eval set but takes about 3 seconds, while the product SLA requires under 800 ms at p95. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Keep the current model and stream the output so callers hear routing begin sooner.
Move intent routing to the Message Batches API to cut the cost of each classification.
Add chain-of-thought instructions so the model's routing decisions become more reliable.
Evaluate a smaller, faster model at low effort against the same eval set and the latency SLA.

questions.explanation: Short, well-defined classification is a strong fit for a faster model at low effort, and the decision should be justified by measuring accuracy and p95 latency on the existing eval set. Streaming (A) does not help when the output is a single short label the system must act on. Batch processing (B) is asynchronous and cannot meet a real-time SLA. Adding chain-of-thought (C) increases latency, moving away from the SLA.

questions.question: A law firm needs risk flags extracted from 20,000 contracts in a one-time review that must finish within three days. Accuracy is the top priority, the budget is fixed, and no user is waiting on individual results. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Use the smallest model in real-time requests to keep the per-contract cost as low as possible.
Use a high-capability model at higher effort, submitted through the Message Batches API.
Use a high-capability model at low effort in many parallel real-time requests to finish quickly.
Use a mid-tier model in real-time requests and re-run any contract the model is unsure about.

questions.explanation: When accuracy matters most and latency does not, batch processing lowers cost and processes asynchronously, which frees budget for a stronger model and more effort. The smallest model (A) trades away the accuracy the firm prioritizes. Low effort (C) gives up quality to chase speed the task does not need. Real-time requests with selective re-runs (D) add complexity and cost more than batching without matching the stronger model's accuracy.

questions.question: A software company runs a coding agent in which an orchestrator plans work and several subagents perform narrow lookups such as reading files and summarizing logs. To cut cost, a manager proposes setting effort to low for the orchestrator and every subagent. What is the best response?

options.text: Apply low effort everywhere, since effort only changes response length and does not affect quality.
Keep high effort everywhere, since lowering effort on any agent always degrades the whole system.
Cap max_tokens tightly on every agent instead, which saves cost on each request without having any effect on reasoning quality.
Run an effort sweep on the eval suite per role, likely lowering effort for subagents but not the planner.

questions.explanation: Effort trades thoroughness for token efficiency; low effort is suggested for simple tasks such as subagents, while planning benefits from deeper reasoning, so the setting should be chosen per role and validated on evals. Effort affects thinking and tool calls, not just length, so a blanket low setting (A) risks the planner's quality. Refusing any change (B) ignores real savings. A tight max_tokens cap (C) is a hard limit that can truncate reasoning and responses mid-task.

questions.question: A wealth-management firm's client chat assistant takes 9 seconds to finish typical answers. Users say it feels unresponsive, but answer quality is rated highly and total completion time is acceptable to the business. Each request has a highly dynamic, personalized context with no stable reusable prefix. Which change best addresses the complaint?

options.text: Stream the response so text appears as it is generated, reducing perceived wait without changing quality.
Switch to a smaller model so total generation time drops, accepting some loss of answer quality.
Reduce retrieved context from 20 passages to 3 so the model has less input to process.
Enable prompt caching on the request so repeated content does not have to be processed again.

questions.explanation: The issue is perceived latency, not total time or quality, so streaming is the targeted fix: users see output immediately while the same model produces the same answer. A smaller model (B) and less retrieved context (C) risk the quality users value to fix a problem that is about responsiveness. Prompt caching (D) needs a stable repeated prefix, which this workload lacks.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical company's RAG assistant has a 3-second p95 SLA and currently runs at 1.8 seconds. Adding a reranking stage over 150 candidates adds about 300 ms and, on the team's labeled eval set, substantially cuts retrieval failures. A stakeholder argues the reranker should be dropped because it is 'slower'. How should the architect justify the decision?

options.text: Drop the reranker, since minimizing latency should always come first in a production assistant.
Replace the reranker by sending all 150 candidates directly to the model and letting it sort them.
Keep the reranker, citing the measured accuracy gain and the remaining headroom under the agreed SLA.
Keep the reranker, but halve the size of the retrieval candidate set so the stage wins back most of the latency it adds.

questions.explanation: Configuration decisions should be justified with measured trade-offs against agreed requirements: the reranker improves accuracy substantially and the system stays well within its SLA, so the latency cost is worth paying. Treating latency as always paramount (A) ignores the SLA that defines acceptable latency. Sending 150 candidates to the model (B) increases tokens, cost, and latency, and dilutes the context. Shrinking the candidate pool (D) weakens the recall that makes reranking effective, solving a problem the SLA says does not exist.

questions.question: A consulting firm's multi-agent research system occasionally returns reports that miss obvious information. Production logs capture only each user's question and the final report, and engineers cannot reproduce the failures because runs differ from one another. What should the team add first?

options.text: A larger weekly human review sample of final reports, scored against a quality rubric.
End-to-end tracing that records each agent's tool calls, search queries, and subagent handoffs.
A lower sampling temperature for every agent so that repeated runs become easier to reproduce.
More detailed final-report logging, including timestamps and the model version that wrote each one.

questions.explanation: Agents make dynamic decisions and behave differently across runs, so diagnosing why one missed information requires visibility into the intermediate steps: which searches ran, which tools returned what, and how work was delegated. Reviewing more final reports (A) or logging more about them (D) still hides where the process went wrong. Lowering temperature (C) does not make multi-step agent runs deterministic and gives no insight into the existing failures.

questions.question: A health insurer runs a member-services agent handling about 50,000 conversations a day and wants to detect behavioral regressions using a third-party observability platform. Conversations contain PHI, and the vendor is not approved to receive it. Which monitoring strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Ship full transcripts to the vendor because complete content is required to detect regressions.
Disable production monitoring and rely on pre-release evals, since PHI makes monitoring too risky.
Send a random 1% of full transcripts to the vendor to limit how much PHI leaves the environment.
Export structured metadata to the vendor and keep redacted content in an approved internal store.

questions.explanation: Behavioral regressions can be detected from structured signals such as tool-call sequences, latency, token usage, error rates, and outcome labels without content leaving the approved boundary; full content stays in a compliant internal store for authorized investigation. Sending full transcripts (A) or even a sample (C) still discloses PHI to an unapproved vendor. Turning off monitoring (B) leaves production regressions undetected.

questions.question: A company is rolling Claude Code out to 2,000 engineers. The platform team must report cost and usage per team and track code-edit acceptance rates in its existing OpenTelemetry-compatible monitoring stack. What is the most effective approach?

options.text: Ask each team lead to collect weekly self-reported usage numbers from their engineers.
Write a script that parses each engineer's local session transcripts and uploads summaries.
Configure Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export in managed settings, tagging each team with resource attributes.
Add a CLAUDE.md instruction asking Claude to print a usage summary at the end of every session.

questions.explanation: Claude Code emits OpenTelemetry metrics and events, including cost, token usage, and edit-decision data; administrators can configure export for every user through managed settings and add team identifiers through resource attributes. Self-reporting (A) is unreliable and does not scale. A transcript parser (B) duplicates built-in telemetry with fragile custom code. CLAUDE.md instructions (D) are probabilistic and do not produce aggregated, queryable data.

questions.question: A SaaS provider's monitoring bill tripled after engineers added user ID, session ID, and a hash of each prompt as labels on every latency and token metric for its Claude integration. Dashboards are also slower. What is the best way to restructure the telemetry?

options.text: Keep metrics on low-cardinality dimensions, and put per-user and per-session identifiers on traces and log events.
Remove all labels from the metrics and rely only on global totals for latency and token usage.
Keep every label but reduce the metric export interval from seconds to once per day.
Move all telemetry into the application database so that dashboards can query it directly.

questions.explanation: High-cardinality identifiers multiply the number of metric time series, driving storage cost and query latency; the standard pattern is to aggregate metrics on bounded dimensions such as model, team, or route, and keep per-request identifiers on traces and events, where they support drill-down. Dropping all labels (B) loses useful breakdowns. Daily export (C) destroys timeliness for alerting. Moving telemetry into the application database (D) shifts the load without fixing the data model.

questions.question: A travel company switched its booking agent to a new model version for all traffic at once. A drop in booking completion surfaced only days later through customer complaints. Which TWO monitoring strategies would have caught the regression early? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Track only latency and API error rates, since quality regressions always show up as errors.
Have a product manager read about ten conversations every week and flag anything suspicious.
Roll out new versions gradually, comparing outcome metrics such as completion rate by version label.
Set temperature to zero on the new model so its behavior is identical to the previous version.
Score a sample of production conversations with automated graders and alert on drift per version.

questions.explanation: A gradual rollout that compares business outcomes by version exposes a regression while only a slice of traffic is affected, and automated grading of sampled production traffic with drift alerts catches quality changes that do not show up as errors. Latency and error dashboards (A) miss answers that are wrong but well-formed. Ten conversations a week (B) is far too small a sample at production scale. Temperature zero (D) does not make a new model behave like the old one.

questions.question: An airline's HR team wants a Q&A assistant over its employee policy handbook, about 120,000 tokens in total, which is updated a few times a year. An engineer has started designing a vector database, a chunking pipeline, and a reranker. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Proceed with the vector pipeline but use smaller chunks, so retrieval stays precise as the handbook grows.
Place the whole handbook in the prompt and use prompt caching, skipping retrieval for a corpus this size.
Fine-tune a model on the handbook so answers come from the model itself and no retrieval is needed.
Build hybrid lexical and semantic search from the start so exact policy numbers are always matched.

questions.explanation: For a knowledge base under roughly 200,000 tokens, Anthropic's guidance is that including the whole corpus in the prompt, with prompt caching to control cost and latency, is often simpler and better than RAG. A retrieval pipeline (A, D) adds components and failure modes the corpus size does not justify. Fine-tuning (C) is costly, hard to update, and not a reliable way to make a model recall specific policy text.

questions.question: An asset manager's RAG system over SEC filings retrieves chunks like 'revenue grew 3% over the prior quarter' with no indication of which company or quarter they describe, so answers mix up issuers. What is the most effective change to the indexing pipeline?

options.text: Increase chunk size to about 4,000 tokens so each chunk is more likely to include the company name.
Retrieve the top 100 chunks instead of the top 20 so the right issuer's chunk is somewhere in context.
Prepend a short, model-generated context to each chunk before embedding and building the keyword index.
Switch to a higher-dimensional embedding model so similar passages from different issuers separate better.

questions.explanation: Contextual retrieval addresses chunks that lose their surrounding context by prepending a brief, document-aware description, such as the company and period, before embedding and BM25 indexing, which significantly reduces retrieval failures. Very large chunks (A) dilute relevance and still may not carry the identifiers. Raising top-k (B) adds noise and cost without making chunks distinguishable. Higher dimensions (D) cannot recover information the chunk text does not contain.

questions.question: A manufacturer indexes equipment manuals that contain multi-step maintenance procedures and torque-specification tables. Fixed 512-token chunking regularly splits tables and procedures in the middle, and answers omit steps or misread values. Which chunking strategy fits best?

options.text: Keep 512-token chunks but raise the overlap between neighbouring chunks to 50 percent.
Reduce chunk size to 128 tokens so each chunk carries one precise fact about a procedure.
Add a reranker after retrieval so the most relevant fragment of each procedure is ranked first.
Chunk on document structure, keeping each procedure and table intact and tagging section metadata.

questions.explanation: When content has meaningful structure, chunk boundaries should follow it, keeping each procedure and table intact and attaching section metadata so retrieval returns complete, usable units. Heavy overlap (A) duplicates content and still splits long units. Tiny chunks (B) fragment procedures further. A reranker (C) can only reorder the broken fragments it is given; it cannot reassemble them.

questions.question: A telecom's sales assistant answers pricing questions from a knowledge base where plan prices change several times a day. The index is rebuilt in full every night, a job that takes 10 hours, so answers are often based on yesterday's prices. Which indexing strategy best addresses the staleness?

options.text: Index incrementally on change events, re-embedding updated documents and deleting superseded chunks.
Provision a larger indexing cluster so the full nightly rebuild completes in two hours instead of ten.
Instruct the assistant to warn users that the prices it quotes may be out of date and should be checked.
Raise the retrieval cache lifetime so that frequently asked pricing questions return the same answer.

questions.explanation: When source data changes frequently, incremental indexing keyed on document IDs and versions keeps the index fresh within minutes and removes outdated chunks so they cannot be retrieved. A faster full rebuild (B) still leaves a daily staleness window and wastes compute re-embedding unchanged content. A warning (C) shifts the problem to users. A longer cache lifetime (D) makes staleness worse.

questions.question: A legal-tech company's case-law search uses a general-purpose embedding model, and evaluation shows poor recall on queries that use legal terminology. Which next step is most appropriate?

options.text: Generate embeddings with Claude through the Messages API, since Claude understands legal language well.
Increase the embedding dimension of the current model so that legal terms get more representational space.
Evaluate a domain-specific legal embedding model on a labeled query set, then re-embed the corpus if it wins.
Pass more retrieved passages to Claude so that relevant cases are eventually included in the context.

questions.explanation: Domain-specific embedding models exist for areas such as law, finance, and code, and the decision to switch should rest on a labeled retrieval evaluation, followed by re-embedding the corpus so queries and documents share one vector space. Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model, so option A is not available. A larger dimension (B) does not fix a model that lacks domain knowledge. More passages (D) treats a recall problem by adding noise and cost.

questions.question: An enterprise software vendor's support assistant uses embedding-only search. Many customer queries contain exact identifiers such as 'ERR-4471' or SKU numbers, and the relevant articles are often missed even though they contain those exact strings. What retrieval change fits best?

options.text: Use smaller chunks so each error code sits in its own short chunk and has a more distinct embedding.
Ask Claude to rewrite each query into a natural-language description before running semantic search.
Combine lexical BM25 search with embedding search and merge the two result lists by rank fusion.
Increase top-k for the embedding search from 20 to 200 so the matching article is eventually returned.

questions.explanation: Exact-match identifiers are where lexical methods like BM25 excel and embeddings are weak, so hybrid retrieval with rank fusion captures both exact identifiers and semantic matches. Smaller chunks (A) do not make embeddings precise about arbitrary codes. Rewriting queries into prose (B) can drop the identifiers that matter most. Raising top-k (D) floods the context with noise and still relies on a method that does not reward exact matches.

questions.question: A retail chain's analysts ask the assistant questions such as 'What were total refunds by region last quarter?' The team embedded each row of the refunds table into a vector store, and the answers are consistently wrong. What is the best redesign?

options.text: Give Claude a read-only query tool over the warehouse so it can compute aggregates directly in SQL.
Embed pre-aggregated monthly summaries instead of individual rows so fewer vectors need to be retrieved.
Increase top-k so that more of the relevant rows are retrieved and passed to the model for summing.
Switch to a larger embedding model so that numeric values in rows are represented more accurately.

questions.explanation: Aggregations over structured data are a query problem, not a similarity-search problem; a read-only query tool lets the database compute exact totals while Claude handles the question and explanation. Embedded summaries (B) only answer the questions anticipated in advance. Retrieving more rows (C) still yields an incomplete sample and asks the model to do arithmetic over partial data. Better embeddings (D) do not make vector search compute totals.

questions.question: An automaker's quality team asks questions such as 'Which suppliers of the brake caliper assembly failed audits last year?' Answering requires finding the component's suppliers in one set of documents and then their audit results in another. Single-shot top-k retrieval often returns only one half. Which approach fits this query pattern?

options.text: Increase top-k so that both supplier and audit documents are more likely to appear in a single retrieval pass.
Merge supplier and audit documents into very large combined chunks so each chunk holds both halves.
Let Claude search iteratively with a search tool, issuing follow-up queries based on what it has found.
Build a full knowledge graph of all suppliers, parts, and audits before allowing any queries to run.

questions.explanation: Multi-hop questions need the second query to depend on the first result, which an agentic loop with a search tool handles naturally. A larger top-k (A) still runs one query that cannot know which suppliers to look up. Merging documents into giant chunks (B) degrades relevance and does not scale. A full knowledge graph (D) may help eventually but is a large up-front investment when iterative retrieval over the existing index solves the pattern.

questions.question: A government agency's policy search returns relevant documents, but the best match is often ranked below weaker ones, and several superseded versions of the same policy crowd the top results. Which TWO changes best improve what reaches the model? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Raise the model's sampling temperature so it considers a wider range of retrieved documents.
Rerank a larger candidate set with a reranking model and pass only the top results to Claude.
Pass only the single highest-scoring chunk to Claude so that weaker documents cannot distract it.
Switch to a larger generation model so it can ignore superseded policies on its own.
Filter candidates on metadata such as status and effective date to exclude superseded versions.

questions.explanation: Reranking a broad candidate set fixes ordering problems that first-stage retrieval leaves behind, and metadata filtering removes superseded versions deterministically before they compete for slots. Temperature (A) affects generation, not retrieval quality. A single chunk (C) sacrifices recall and may still be the wrong version. A larger model (D) is asked to compensate for retrieval problems it cannot reliably detect.

questions.question: An engineering organization wants an assistant that answers questions about a large monorepo that receives hundreds of commits a day. Questions often reference exact function names and error strings. Which retrieval strategy best matches this data and query pattern?

options.text: Embed the entire repository nightly and run semantic search over that day's snapshot of the code.
Let the agent search the live repository just in time with tools such as grep and glob, then read files.
Load the whole repository into the context window at the start of every conversation with the assistant.
Fine-tune a model on the repository each week so that it learns the structure of the code base directly.

questions.explanation: Rapidly changing code with exact-identifier queries suits just-in-time agentic search: grep and glob are always current and match exact strings, and the agent reads only the files it needs, which is how Claude Code works. A nightly embedding index (A) goes stale within hours and handles exact identifiers poorly. A large monorepo will not fit in context (C), and weekly fine-tuning (D) is costly, stale, and does not support precise lookups.

questions.question: A media company wants its internal ticketing system to be usable from Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and its own Claude Agent SDK application, with consistent behavior and centrally managed authentication. Which integration mechanism fits best?

options.text: Write separate custom tool definitions for each of the three products and keep them in sync manually.
Build one remote MCP server for the ticketing system, secured with OAuth, and connect all three clients.
Publish a command-line wrapper for the ticketing API and require every client to call it through a shell.
Deploy a dedicated ticketing agent and have each product delegate to it over an agent-to-agent protocol.

questions.explanation: MCP is designed for exactly this: one server exposes the ticketing capabilities once, and any MCP host, such as Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or an Agent SDK app, can connect to it, with the remote Streamable HTTP transport and OAuth providing central authentication. Separate tool definitions (A) duplicate work and drift apart. A CLI wrapper (C) does not work in clients without a shell. An agent-to-agent design (D) adds a whole autonomous agent where a simple capability interface is enough.

questions.question: A distributor runs a nightly job that sends each invoice PDF to Claude to extract a fixed set of fields, then writes the result into its ERP. The steps never vary and no model judgment is needed about which system to call. Which integration approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Build an MCP server for the ERP and let an agent decide when and how to write each extracted invoice.
Call the Claude API directly from the pipeline code and write to the ERP's API from that same code.
Run Claude Code in headless mode with an ERP MCP server and a prompt that describes the whole job.
Create an extraction agent and an ERP agent that coordinate with each other over an agent-to-agent protocol.

questions.explanation: A fixed, deterministic workflow is best implemented as code that calls the Claude API for extraction and the ERP API for writes, keeping control flow predictable and testable. Giving an agent the ERP through MCP (A, C) introduces model-driven decisions where none are needed. Two coordinating agents (D) is the most over-engineered option for a fixed pipeline.

questions.question: A manufacturer's procurement agent needs to hand shipment requests to a logistics partner's autonomous agent, which runs its own models, tools, and policies. The exchange involves multi-turn negotiation and status updates over several days, and the partner will not expose its internal systems. Which integration mechanism fits best?

options.text: Ask the partner to provide read and write credentials to its shipping database for the procurement agent.
Use computer use to have the procurement agent operate the partner's web portal like a human user would.
Ask the partner to expose every internal logistics tool as an MCP server the procurement agent calls directly.
Use an agent-to-agent protocol, treating the partner's agent as an opaque peer that accepts and updates tasks.

questions.explanation: When the counterparty is an independently operated agent that owns its own reasoning and will not expose internals, an agent-to-agent protocol suits long-running, multi-turn task delegation between peers. Direct database credentials (A) violate the partner's boundary and least privilege. Driving a web portal (B) is brittle and slow for a multi-day negotiation. MCP (C) is meant for exposing tools and data to an agent, which the partner has declined to do.

questions.question: A platform team wants Claude Code to open pull requests, read review comments, and check CI status on GitHub. The gh CLI is already installed and authenticated on every developer machine. An engineer proposes building a custom GitHub MCP server first. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Build the custom MCP server, because Claude Code can only interact with external services through MCP.
Use computer use so that Claude Code operates github.com in a browser exactly as a developer would.
Let Claude Code use the existing gh CLI, with permission rules that allow the specific commands needed.
Have developers paste pull request details and CI logs into the session whenever they are needed.

questions.explanation: Claude Code's guidance is that CLI tools such as gh are the most context-efficient way to work with external services, and permission rules can scope exactly which commands are allowed without prompting. Building a custom MCP server (A) duplicates a capability that already exists, and Claude Code is not limited to MCP. Browser automation (B) is slow and brittle. Manual pasting (D) defeats the automation goal.

questions.question: A global bank's employee assistant connects to 12 MCP servers exposing about 300 tools, whose definitions consume roughly 70,000 tokens before any work starts. Tool-selection accuracy has fallen as servers were added. Which strategy best addresses both problems?

options.text: Shorten every tool description to a single line so that all 300 definitions fit in fewer tokens.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so all tool definitions fit with room to spare.
Route each request to one of 12 separate agents, each preloaded with one server's tools, by keyword.
Enable tool search with deferred loading, keeping the few most-used tools loaded on every request.

questions.explanation: Tool search defers tool definitions until Claude discovers them, cutting definition overhead dramatically and keeping selection accurate, since accuracy degrades past roughly 30 to 50 loaded tools; keeping the three to five most frequent tools non-deferred avoids search overhead for common work. One-line descriptions (A) make selection harder. A bigger context window (B) fixes neither the cost nor the accuracy problem. Keyword routing to 12 agents (C) adds brittle orchestration and fails on requests that span servers.

questions.question: A startup's invoicing agent has six tools whose definitions total about 800 tokens, and every request uses most of them. An engineer proposes enabling tool search with deferred loading for all six to follow 'best practice'. What is the best response?

options.text: Adopt it, since deferred loading always lowers cost and improves accuracy regardless of tool count.
Adopt it, but defer only half of the six tools so that the agent searches less often than before.
Decline it, since loading a small set of tools that every request uses is the simpler and better fit.
Decline it, and instead merge all six tools into a single generic tool to minimize definitions further.

questions.explanation: Progressive discovery pays off when there are many tools or large definitions; with fewer than 10 small tools that are used on nearly every request, loading them up front is simpler and avoids an extra search step. Adopting it for its own sake (A, B) adds latency and complexity for no measurable benefit. Merging distinct operations into one generic tool (D) blurs tool boundaries and makes tool choice and arguments less clear.

questions.question: A property insurer's claims agents follow 40 internal procedures, each 3,000 to 8,000 tokens, and any given claim needs only one or two. Today every procedure is pasted into the system prompt, and the team is near the context limit with rising cost. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Summarize each procedure down to about 200 tokens so all 40 fit comfortably in the system prompt.
Package each procedure as a Skill, so only short descriptions load up front and full text loads on use.
Fine-tune a model on all 40 procedures so the agent no longer needs them in its context at all.
Split the claims agent into 40 specialist agents, each with one procedure in its system prompt.

questions.explanation: Skills use progressive disclosure: only each Skill's name and description, about 100 tokens, load at startup, and the full instructions load only when a task matches, so 40 procedures cost little until they are needed. Aggressive summaries (A) discard the procedural detail the agents rely on. Fine-tuning (C) is costly to maintain and unreliable for exact procedures. Forty specialist agents (D) need a routing layer and complicate claims that touch two procedures.

questions.question: A law firm is designing a hybrid context strategy for a litigation research agent working on one matter at a time. Which TWO items should be loaded into context up front rather than discovered on demand? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The firm's citation-format rules, which apply to every answer the agent produces.
The full text of the firm's 3,000-case precedent library that might be relevant to the matter.
Every document in the matter's discovery set, so nothing relevant can be missed by search.
A short key-facts summary of the current matter that the agent refers to on most turns.
Definitions for all 200 tools across the firm's document, billing, and research systems.

questions.explanation: A hybrid strategy loads small, always-relevant context up front, such as formatting rules applied to every answer and a compact matter summary used on most turns, and retrieves large or occasionally needed material just in time. The precedent library (B) and the discovery set (C) are large corpora that belong behind search. Loading 200 tool definitions (E) is exactly the bloat that deferred tool loading avoids.

questions.question: An insurer's claims director asks you to "make sure the new claim-summary assistant is high quality" before launch. Adjusters will rely on the summaries to decide whether a claim needs escalation. Which success criterion should you propose to the stakeholders?

options.text: Summaries should read clearly and professionally, as judged informally by the claims team lead during a one-week pilot.
At least 95% of summaries on a labeled 500-claim set capture every escalation-relevant fact, scored with an adjuster-approved rubric.
The assistant should match the quality of the best human adjuster's summaries across every claim type from launch day.
Summaries should be as short as possible, since a lower average token count signals focused, higher-quality output.

questions.explanation: A good success criterion is specific, measurable, achievable, and tied to the business purpose, and B states a numeric target on a representative labeled set using a rubric the business owns. An informal pilot judgment (A) is neither repeatable nor measurable. Matching the best human on every claim type at launch (C) is not grounded in any baseline and is unlikely to be achievable. Brevity (D) measures the wrong thing; a short summary that drops an escalation trigger is a failure.

questions.question: A retailer's support assistant was tuned only for answer accuracy. After launch, accuracy improved, but finance reports that spend tripled and customers complain about long waits. Leadership wants the evaluation scorecard revised so a release like this cannot pass again. Which TWO additions best address the gap? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Average words per response, minimized and adopted as the new primary quality metric for releases.
A larger set of accuracy test cases, so that the accuracy estimate becomes statistically more precise.
Cost per resolved conversation, measured on the eval set against an agreed budget threshold.
The number of tools available to the agent, maximized so the assistant can cover more request types.
p95 latency per conversation turn, measured on the eval set with a target tied to the support SLA.

questions.explanation: Production LLM systems need multidimensional criteria, and this release failed on cost and latency, which the scorecard never measured. Cost per resolved conversation (C) and p95 latency against the SLA (E) turn those business constraints into release gates. Minimizing word count (A) is a proxy that can hurt quality without capturing cost or latency directly. More accuracy cases (B) sharpen the one metric that was already being tracked, and maximizing tool count (D) tends to add tokens and latency rather than control them.

questions.question: A hospital network's scheduling assistant must never reveal one patient's health information to another caller. The compliance officer asks how the team will know the assistant is safe enough to launch. Which approach gives a defensible answer?

options.text: Instruct Claude in the system prompt never to disclose health information, and treat that instruction as the safety control.
Have three clinicians chat with the assistant for an afternoon and sign off if none of them notices a disclosure.
Track the overall patient satisfaction score after launch and treat any drop as the signal that leaks are occurring.
Grade a large adversarial and representative test set with a binary leak check and set a launch threshold for leak rate.

questions.explanation: Safety becomes a usable metric when it is quantified over enough cases, for example a leak rate measured by a binary classifier across a large set that includes adversarial attempts, with an agreed threshold. A prompt instruction (A) is a control, not a measurement of whether it works. An afternoon of manual chats (B) is far too small and unstructured to estimate a rare failure rate. Satisfaction scores (C) are lagging, indirect, and would detect a leak only after harm has occurred.

questions.question: A bank's customer-facing dispute agent completes about 80% of tasks correctly when each task is run once. The product owner wants a metric that reflects whether customers will get a correct outcome every time they make the same kind of request. What should the team report?

options.text: pass^k: run each task k times and count it as passed only if every one of the k trials succeeds.
pass@k: run each task k times and count it as passed if at least one of the k trials succeeds.
Mean BLEU score of the agent's replies against reference replies written by the disputes team.
Single-run accuracy averaged across tasks, since repeating a task adds no information about the agent.

questions.explanation: pass^k measures the probability that all k trials succeed, so it captures consistency and falls as k grows, which is what a customer-facing agent needs. pass@k (B) rises with k and answers a different question, whether any attempt can solve the task, which suits tools where one good result is enough. BLEU against references (C) measures textual overlap, not whether the dispute was handled correctly. Single-run accuracy (D) ignores non-determinism; the same task can pass on one run and fail on the next.

questions.question: An accounts-payable agent reads inbound vendor emails and can open payment-detail change tickets. The security team wants a metric that shows how well the agent resists prompt injection before each release. Which metric should you define?

options.text: The count of suspicious keywords caught by an input filter each week, reported as the injection-defense metric for the agent.
The agent's overall task accuracy on normal vendor emails, on the assumption that an accurate agent also resists manipulation.
Attack success rate on a curated suite of injected emails that try to trigger unauthorized tickets, paired with the false-refusal rate on benign emails.
The number of security reviews completed on the system prompt, with each review sign-off counted as evidence of resistance.

questions.explanation: A security metric should measure the outcome you are defending against: the share of realistic attack inputs that achieve an unauthorized action, measured on a maintained suite, balanced by a false-refusal rate so the defense does not simply block normal work. Keyword hits (A) count filter activity, not whether attacks succeed. Accuracy on benign emails (B) says nothing about adversarial behavior. Review counts (D) measure process activity rather than system behavior.

questions.question: A contract-intake pipeline extracts party names, effective dates, and amounts into JSON, and also writes a short plain-language summary for the business owner. You need an evaluation that is reliable and can run on every prompt change. Which TWO grading approaches should you use? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Have legal staff manually review every extracted field and every summary on each release candidate.
Compare extracted fields to labeled values with code after normalizing formats, plus schema validation.
Use an LLM judge for the extracted fields, because it tolerates formatting differences in dates and amounts.
Compute ROUGE overlap between the JSON output and the source contract text to score extraction quality.
Use an LLM judge with a specific rubric for the summaries, spot-checked against a human-graded sample.

questions.explanation: Mixed methods match each grader to the output type: fields with known correct values are best graded by deterministic code after normalization (B), while open-ended summaries need a rubric-driven LLM judge whose scores are calibrated against human grading (E). Full manual review (A) is too slow to run on every change. Using an LLM judge for fields (C) adds non-determinism where an exact check is available. ROUGE against the source text (D) measures overlap with the contract, not whether the extracted values are right.

questions.question: A team built an LLM judge that scores support replies from 1 to 5 for empathy. Dashboards show a steady 4.6 average, yet customer comments increasingly describe the replies as robotic. What should the team do first?

options.text: Have humans grade a sample of the same replies, measure their agreement with the judge, and revise the rubric until the two align.
Switch the judge to the most capable model available, since a stronger grader will automatically match human perception of tone.
Raise the judge's passing threshold from 4 to 5 so that only the most empathetic replies are counted as passing.
Replace the empathy judge with a word-count metric, since longer replies are generally perceived as more caring.

questions.explanation: Model-based graders handle nuance but must be calibrated against human judgment, and a gap between judge scores and customer perception means the judge is not measuring what matters. Comparing against a human-graded sample shows where the rubric is wrong. A more capable grader (B) still applies the same flawed rubric. Raising the threshold (C) rescales a miscalibrated score without fixing it. Word count (D) is a crude proxy that could reward padding rather than empathy.

questions.question: A research assistant has a web search tool. Its eval set contains only questions that require fresh information. After several rounds of tuning against it, the agent now searches even for simple arithmetic and definitions, adding latency and cost. How should the team fix the evaluation?

options.text: Remove the web search tool from the agent so that it can no longer over-use searching on any question.
Add more current-events questions so the eval set better reflects how often users need a search.
Tighten the eval's latency budget so that slow responses fail regardless of whether their final answers are correct and complete.
Add cases where searching is unnecessary and grade them on answering directly, so the suite rewards searching only when needed.

questions.explanation: An eval that only tests when a behavior should happen leads to one-sided optimization, so a balanced set must also include cases where the behavior should not happen. Adding no-search-needed cases (D) lets the score reward correct judgment about when to search. Removing the tool (A) breaks the questions that genuinely need fresh data. More current-events questions (B) make the imbalance worse. A tighter latency budget (C) penalizes legitimate searches as well and does not teach the distinction.

questions.question: A legal-tech team iterates on a contract-review prompt daily. Their only evaluation is 40 cases, each graded by a senior attorney, and one grading round takes two weeks. Which evaluation strategy best supports their iteration speed?

options.text: Keep the 40 attorney-graded cases as the only release gate, since expert judgment gives the highest-quality signal available to the team.
Delay all evaluation until the prompt is final, then run a single large attorney review just before launch.
Build several hundred automatically graded cases for daily runs, and reserve attorney review for a periodic calibration sample.
Drop pre-release evaluation and collect attorney feedback from production after each deploy instead.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance favors volume with automated grading over a small number of hand-graded cases, keeping human experts for calibration. A large automated set (C) gives fast feedback on every change, while periodic attorney review keeps the graders honest. A two-week, 40-case gate (A) cannot keep up with daily changes. Evaluating only at the end (B) removes feedback from the iteration loop. Production-only feedback (D) exposes clients to regressions before anyone measures them.

questions.question: An internal IT helpdesk agent has been live for three months with no eval set. The team proposes spending a quarter generating 2,000 synthetic test cases before evaluating anything. What is the better way to start?

options.text: Delay evaluation until all 2,000 synthetic cases exist, since small sets produce results too noisy to act on.
Start with a few dozen tasks drawn from real tickets the agent mishandled, and grow the set as new failures appear.
Adopt a public IT-support benchmark as the eval set so results can be compared directly across vendors.
Have Claude generate the cases from the system prompt alone, since the prompt already defines everything the agent should do.

questions.explanation: Teams can begin with roughly 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures and bug reports, because early changes have large effects that small sets can detect, and real failures reflect the actual task distribution. Waiting a quarter (A) leaves the live system unmeasured. A public benchmark (C) does not reflect this company's tickets, systems, or policies. Cases generated only from the system prompt (D) test what the designers already anticipated rather than how real users break the agent.

questions.question: A travel-booking agent's eval asserts the exact sequence of tool calls for each task. A new prompt version fails 30% of tasks because the agent checks seat availability before fare rules, yet every resulting booking in the sandbox is correct. What should the team change?

options.text: Grade the end state, such as whether a correct booking with valid fare rules exists in the sandbox, instead of the exact call sequence.
Revert the prompt change, since any deviation from the expected tool-call sequence indicates a regression in the agent.
Add prompt instructions forcing the agent to always call its tools in exactly the order that the tests expect.
Lower the eval's pass threshold to 70% so the new prompt version can ship despite the reported failures.

questions.explanation: Agent evals should generally grade what the agent achieved rather than the exact path it took, because rigid path checks penalize valid alternative solutions. Checking the final booking state (A) measures the real requirement. Reverting (B) and forcing a call order (C) optimize the agent for the test rather than for correct outcomes. Lowering the threshold (D) hides the grader flaw and would also let genuine failures through.

questions.question: A loan-servicing chatbot in a regulated lender has two candidate system prompts. The product manager wants to A/B test both on live customer traffic at a 50/50 split starting tomorrow. Inaccurate answers about loan terms carry regulatory risk. What should you recommend?

options.text: Launch the 50/50 A/B test immediately, since live customer traffic is the only valid signal of real outcomes.
Pick the prompt the product manager prefers after reading a few sample responses, and skip the A/B test.
Run the A/B test on internal employees only, then ship the winner to all customers without further checks.
Run both prompts through the offline eval suite first, then A/B test only passing candidates at a small traffic share with guardrail metrics.

questions.explanation: Offline evals catch regressions cheaply before customers see them, and online A/B tests then measure real user outcomes; in a regulated setting the online test should start small and carry guardrail metrics. Going straight to a 50/50 live split (A) exposes half of customers to an unvetted prompt. Choosing by reading a few samples (B) is anecdotal. Employee-only testing (C) does not represent customer queries, and shipping its winner without checks skips both safety gates.

questions.question: An e-commerce team is A/B testing a new product-recommendation prompt. They randomize per request, so one shopper can see both variants within a single conversation, and they plan to declare a winner as soon as any metric reaches significance. How should the test be redesigned?

options.text: Keep per-request randomization and check results daily, stopping the test as soon as click-through differs significantly.
Compare this month's conversion with last month's under the old prompt, avoiding a traffic split altogether.
Assign variants per user, predefine one primary metric plus guardrails, and fix the sample size before reading results.
Serve the new prompt to VIP customers and the old prompt to everyone else, then compare conversion between them.

questions.explanation: A sound A/B test keeps each user in one variant so experiences do not mix, names its primary and guardrail metrics in advance, and fixes the sample size to avoid false positives from repeated peeking across many metrics. Per-request assignment with early stopping (A) contaminates the comparison and inflates false wins. A month-over-month comparison (B) confounds the prompt with seasonality and traffic changes. Splitting by customer tier (D) confounds the prompt with differences between the groups.

questions.question: In a single release, a team moved to a different model tier, rewrote the system prompt, and changed the retrieval top-k from 5 to 20. The eval score dropped by 6 points. What should they do next?

options.text: Revert all three changes and abandon the release, since the combination has clearly made the overall system worse.
Test each change in isolation against the baseline on the same eval set to attribute the drop to its cause.
Keep all three changes and add more few-shot examples to the prompt until the score recovers to baseline.
Ship the release anyway, since a 6-point drop is within the normal variation of LLM-generated outputs.

questions.explanation: Iterative improvement depends on attributing effects to causes, and three simultaneous changes make that impossible. Ablating each change against the same baseline (B) shows which one hurt and keeps any that helped. Reverting everything (A) may discard a beneficial change. Patching with few-shot examples (C) treats the symptom without knowing the cause. Assuming a 6-point drop is noise (D) is unjustified without repeated trials showing the run-to-run variance.

questions.question: A new prompt scored 82% versus the current prompt's 79% on a 40-case eval, with each case run once. The team wants to announce the improvement to stakeholders today. What should happen first?

options.text: Run several trials per case for both prompts and compare their success rates and variability before drawing a conclusion.
Announce the improvement to stakeholders now, since any increase on the eval set reflects a real gain in production quality.
Re-run only the cases the new prompt failed until each one passes, and then report the improved final score.
Remove the cases where the two prompts disagree, since they are ambiguous and distort the comparison.

questions.explanation: Model outputs vary between runs, so a 3-point gap on 40 single-run cases may be noise; multiple trials per task give a success rate and a sense of variance before you claim a win. Announcing immediately (B) risks reporting a gain that disappears. Re-running failures until they pass (C) cherry-picks results. Removing disagreement cases (D) discards exactly the cases that distinguish the two prompts.

questions.question: A ticket-classification eval has sat at 99% for months, and three new prompt variants all score 99% on it. Meanwhile, production escalations reveal new misclassification patterns the eval does not include. How should the team proceed?

options.text: Conclude that the prompt is already optimal and stop iterating, since the eval shows there is no room left to improve.
Raise the pass threshold to 99.5% so that the small differences between the prompt variants become visible.
Delete the eval entirely, since a saturated suite provides no value and only slows down the CI pipeline.
Keep the saturated suite as a regression gate and build a harder capability set from the new production failures.

questions.explanation: A saturated eval can no longer show improvement, but it still protects against regressions, so it should continue as a regression suite while a new, harder capability set is built from real failures. Stopping iteration (A) ignores clear evidence of unmeasured failures. A higher threshold (B) only magnifies noise on cases the model already passes. Deleting the suite (C) throws away regression protection.

questions.question: A compliance assistant answers employee questions from 80-page policy documents placed in context. Reviewers find that it sometimes cites clause numbers that do not exist in the policy. Which TWO changes most directly reduce this behavior? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Instruct Claude to first extract verbatim quotes relevant to the question and base its answer only on those quotes.
Increase max_tokens so that the model has more room to produce thorough and complete answers.
Add general background on compliance regulations to the system prompt so the model can draw on more domain knowledge.
Explicitly allow Claude to say that the policy does not address the question when no supporting text exists.
Ask for answers in a confident, authoritative tone to discourage vague hedging in responses.

questions.explanation: Grounding answers in direct quotes extracted from long documents (A) and explicitly permitting the model to admit when the source lacks an answer (D) are documented techniques for reducing hallucinations. More output room (B) does not address fabrication. Extra general background (C) invites answers from general knowledge instead of the policy. Demanding a confident tone (E) discourages the model from signaling uncertainty, which tends to increase confident errors.

questions.question: A financial analyst assistant runs on the fastest, lowest-cost model tier at low effort. Evals show strong results on single-step lookups but frequent errors on multi-step reconciliations across several statements. The prompt has been reviewed and is clear. What is the best next step?

options.text: Add more few-shot examples of single-step lookups, which reinforces the pattern the model already handles well.
Shorten the prompt so the smaller model has more of its capacity left over for reasoning about each task.
Evaluate the failing reconciliation slice on a more capable model or higher effort, and route that task type accordingly.
Move the entire workload to the most capable model at maximum effort, regardless of how well the lookup slice already performs.

questions.explanation: Failures concentrated in the complex slice, with a clear prompt, point to a model or effort mismatch for that task type rather than a prompt failure. Testing that slice on a stronger configuration and routing it there (C) fixes the problem without raising cost on the lookups that already work. More lookup examples (A) target the wrong slice. Shortening a clear prompt (B) does not add reasoning capability. Moving everything to the top tier at maximum effort (D) overspends on the simple majority.

questions.question: An invoice-extraction service intermittently returns JSON that fails to parse. Failures cluster on the longest invoices, and the logs show a stop_reason of "max_tokens" on every failed request. What is the root-cause fix?

options.text: Switch to a larger model, since the parse failures show that the current model cannot reliably produce valid JSON output.
Raise max_tokens to fit the largest invoices, and handle a max_tokens stop reason as truncation rather than success.
Add an instruction stressing that the output must always be valid JSON with no trailing commas or comments.
Retry each failed request until it parses, since malformed JSON is a random artifact of sampling.

questions.explanation: A max_tokens stop reason means the response hit the output limit and was cut off, which explains broken JSON on the longest inputs. Raising the limit and treating that stop reason as truncation (B) fixes the cause and prevents silent failures. A larger model (A) and stricter formatting instructions (C) do not change the output limit. Blind retries (D) will truncate at the same point again and waste spend.
