Demo recordings and raw chat archives contain little actionable guidance and are hard to use. A list of tried variants without results gives no basis for decisions.

questions.question: In a mature deployment, system prompts live as string constants in the code with no explanation. Engineers have twice removed sentences that looked redundant, and each time a compliance behavior silently broke. What practice best prevents this?

options.text: Version prompts as reviewed artifacts with notes explaining why each section exists, and run evals on every change.
Lock the prompts so that only the original architect is permitted to edit them from now on going forward.
Move the prompts into a shared document that business stakeholders can edit directly whenever they wish.
Add a code comment at the top of the file telling engineers not to touch the prompt under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: Prompts are part of the system's behavior and need the same documentation and change control as code. Recording why each instruction exists tells future maintainers what a deletion would break, and running the evaluation suite on each change catches regressions before release. Locking prompts to one person creates a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Moving prompts to an editable document removes review entirely. A do-not-touch comment explains nothing and blocks legitimate improvement.

questions.question: After handoff, the client's engineers will extend your integration service using Claude Code. You want them, and Claude Code, to follow the architecture's conventions: the service boundaries, the build and test commands, and the rule that all model calls go through one gateway module. Where should this guidance live?

options.text: In a personal CLAUDE.md file in your own home directory, since you are the architect who wrote the conventions.
In a slide deck from the final handoff meeting, which engineers can consult when they have a question later.
In a separate email to each engineer, so that everyone receives the guidance directly in their own inbox.
In a project CLAUDE.md checked into the repository, with hooks for any rule that must be strictly enforced.

questions.explanation: A project-level CLAUDE.md committed to the repository is shared with everyone who works on the code and is loaded into every Claude Code session, so conventions travel with the code. Because CLAUDE.md is treated as context rather than enforced configuration, rules that must never be broken are better backed by hooks or checks. A personal file in the architect's home directory does not reach the client team. Slide decks and emails are disconnected from the code and quickly go stale.

questions.question: A clinical documentation summarizer you built for administrative staff was later reused by another department to support treatment decisions, a use it was never evaluated for. When documenting future systems, which TWO elements most directly reduce this risk? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: A clear statement of intended use, intended users, and uses that are explicitly out of scope.
The full system prompt published to every end user, so that anyone can see how the tool works.
Evaluation results and known failure modes, with the conditions under which the system was tested.
A summary of the model provider's marketing materials describing the model's general capabilities.
An org chart listing the names of the team members who built the system and their current roles.

questions.explanation: Documenting intended use and explicit out-of-scope uses tells downstream teams where the system is and is not appropriate. Publishing evaluation results, test conditions, and known failure modes shows what evidence exists, so a team considering a new use can see that it has not been validated. Publishing the system prompt does not convey suitability for a use. Vendor marketing describes general capability, not this system's validated scope. An org chart does not help anyone judge safe use.

questions.question: Your architecture documentation for a multi-team RAG platform is a single detailed diagram. Executives find it unreadable, and engineers say it lacks the sequence and data-contract detail they need. What is the best fix?

options.text: Add more labels and colors to the existing diagram so that it serves both the executives and the engineers better.
Produce layered views: a context view for business readers and component, sequence, and contract detail for engineers.
Remove the diagrams and tell everyone that the source code is the only reliable architecture documentation.
Let each team write and maintain its own version of the architecture, with no central owner or shared source.

questions.explanation: Different audiences need different levels of abstraction, so layered views from a common model let executives see the system in its business context while engineers get component, sequence, and interface detail. Keeping these views consistent and owned avoids drift. Adding more detail to one diagram makes it worse for executives without fully serving engineers. Code alone does not explain context or rationale to anyone. Unowned per-team versions quickly diverge and contradict each other.

questions.question: Anthropic has notified you that the model behind a client's production underwriting assistant is deprecated and will be retired in about two months. Several teams in the client's organization call the API. What is the best plan?

options.text: Wait until shortly before the retirement date, since deprecated models keep working until then and nothing is urgent.
Change the model ID in production today to the recommended replacement, since newer models are generally better.
Find all usage, run your evals on the replacement, roll out in stages, and tell stakeholders the timeline.
Ask the provider to extend the retirement for this client and pause other migration work until a reply arrives.

questions.explanation: Requests to a retired model fail, so migration must be planned and finished before the retirement date. Anthropic's guidance is to test with the replacement well in advance; the Console usage export, broken down by API key and model, helps find every team still calling the deprecated model. Running your own evals, staging the rollout, and communicating the timeline turns a forced change into a controlled one. Waiting leaves no time to fix regressions. Switching blindly risks behavior changes in a regulated workflow. Pausing for an extension request gambles on an outcome you cannot control.

questions.question: After handoff, the client's operations team monitors a customer-facing Claude assistant using only HTTP error rates and response latency. Two months later, customers complain that answers have become less helpful, but every dashboard is green. What monitoring should have been added during the monitoring phase?

options.text: More granular infrastructure metrics, such as CPU and memory on all the application servers, sampled every second.
A larger alerting budget, so that the operations team is paged on every single HTTP error the system returns.
Daily reviews of full raw logs of every conversation by the operations team, read from start to finish.
Quality signals: sampled outputs scored against the rubric, plus feedback, escalation, and cost-per-task trends.

questions.explanation: LLM systems can degrade in quality while remaining technically healthy, so production monitoring must include quality signals as well as uptime and latency. Scoring a sample of outputs against the agreed rubric and tracking feedback, escalation rates, and cost per task reveals drift early. More infrastructure metrics or more aggressive error paging still measure only technical health. Manually reading every conversation does not scale and offers no consistent signal.

questions.question: In production, a benefits-eligibility assistant gave an incorrect answer for a specific type of dependent coverage question. The team knows how to fix the prompt. In the iteration phase, what should they do before shipping the fix?

options.text: Add the failing case and close variants to the regression eval suite, then confirm the fix passes them without new failures.
Ship the prompt fix right away, since the failure is understood and a delay would affect more users in production.
Ask the reporting user to test the fix manually and ship it as soon as they confirm the answer now looks correct.
Rewrite the entire system prompt from scratch so that the new version avoids this and any similar problems.

questions.explanation: Turning real production failures into evaluation cases means the fix can be verified and the problem cannot quietly return later. Running the full suite also checks that the change has not broken behavior elsewhere. Shipping immediately skips verification of side effects. A single user's manual check covers one case and offers no regression protection. Rewriting the whole prompt introduces far more risk than the targeted fix.

questions.question: You are deciding whether a document-review system is ready to move from your delivery team to the client's operations team. Which TWO conditions are the strongest indicators of handoff readiness? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Your delivery team keeps the only production deployment credentials, so that changes stay controlled.
The system is frozen permanently at handoff, so the client never needs to change prompts or models.
A named client owner is accountable for prompts, evals, and model changes, with authority to release.
The client's on-call staff have practiced the runbook, including a rollback, in a realistic exercise.
The evaluation suite is retired at handoff to reduce the maintenance burden on the receiving team.

questions.explanation: A successful handoff transfers both ownership and capability: someone on the client side must be accountable for the system's prompts, evaluations, and model updates, and the operations staff must have actually practiced the procedures they will rely on. Keeping credentials with the delivery team means the handoff has not really happened. Freezing the system ignores the need to iterate and to migrate as models are retired. Retiring the evaluation suite removes the safety net needed for every future change.

questions.question: A shared Claude platform now serves four business units, and finance wants monthly chargeback reports so each unit's leadership can see and manage its own spend. All units currently share one workspace and one API key. What should you recommend?

options.text: Estimate each unit's share of the bill from its headcount and divide the monthly invoice using that ratio.
Give each unit its own workspace and keys, and report spend by workspace from the Usage and Cost Admin API.
Ask each unit to log token counts from its own application code and email monthly totals to the finance team.
Keep the shared setup and send each unit the organization-wide invoice so all units see the total spend.

questions.explanation: Separating units into their own workspaces and keys makes usage attributable at the source, and the Usage and Cost Admin API can group cost by workspace for chargeback reporting. This gives each unit accurate, ongoing visibility to manage its spend. Headcount ratios are not tied to actual use. Self-reported counts from application code are inconsistent and hard to reconcile with billing. Sharing the total invoice gives no unit the information it needs to act.
